page_title: Acne Treatment for Teens and Adults: When to See a GP
claim_text: Early treatment can reduce scarring and months of frustration. ... Sometimes, but waiting can increase scarring risk.
evidence_summary: Delayed or inadequate treatment of inflammatory/cystic acne is a recognised risk factor for permanent scarring; earlier effective treatment reduces that risk. The copy already uses proportionate 'can reduce'/'can increase' language rather than absolute claims.
limitations: Scarring risk is individual and depends on acne type and severity; benefit of 'early' treatment is supported directionally rather than by a single quantified figure.
reviewer_notes: Wording is proportionate and defensible. No change needed.

page_title: Acne Treatment for Teens and Adults: When to See a GP
claim_text: Acne treatment usually needs patience. Many options take 8 to 12 weeks to show clear improvement, and some can irritate skin at first if started too quickly.
evidence_summary: Standard dermatology guidance is that acne treatments (topical retinoids, topical/oral antibiotics) commonly take 8-12 weeks or longer before clear improvement is seen, and topical retinoids often cause initial irritation. The 8-12 week figure aligns with authoritative sources.
limitations: Timeframe is a general expectation; some regimens take longer than 12 weeks.
reviewer_notes: Specific numeric claim verified. Acceptable.

page_title: Acne Treatment for Teens and Adults: When to See a GP
claim_text: Retinoid: A vitamin A related acne treatment; some forms are not safe in pregnancy. ... referral for isotretinoin when acne is severe, scarring or resistant ... what to avoid in pregnancy.
evidence_summary: Oral isotretinoin is a known teratogen with strict pregnancy-prevention requirements; topical retinoids are generally avoided/cautioned in pregnancy. The article's cautious framing ('some forms are not safe in pregnancy', 'strict safety rules') is accurate and appropriately non-alarming.
limitations: Exact pregnancy-category advice varies by agent; correctly deferred to the GP.
reviewer_notes: Safety framing is accurate and proportionate.

page_title: Acne Treatment for Teens and Adults: When to See a GP
claim_text: Can diet cause acne? Diet may influence acne for some people, but it is rarely the only factor.
evidence_summary: Evidence linking diet to acne is limited and mixed (some association with high-glycaemic-load diets and possibly dairy). The article's hedged 'may influence for some people, rarely the only factor' correctly represents the uncertain evidence and avoids overstatement.
limitations: Diet-acne evidence remains low certainty.
reviewer_notes: Well hedged. Acceptable.

page_title: Acne Treatment for Teens and Adults: When to See a GP
claim_text: Some hormonal contraception can help selected patients, but suitability depends on medical history and side effects.
evidence_summary: Combined hormonal contraception is an accepted second-line option for acne in selected patients. 'Can help selected patients' with a suitability caveat is accurate and appropriately individualised.
limitations: URL for DermNet hormonal-acne page inferred from the same domain; concept verified via general acne guidance.
reviewer_notes: Acceptable; individualised framing preserved.

page_title: Eczema, Psoriasis and Chronic Skin Conditions: Getting a GP Plan
claim_text: Used correctly, topical steroids can be very helpful and safe. Problems are more likely when they are the wrong strength, used in the wrong place, or used without a plan.
evidence_summary: Topical corticosteroids used at appropriate potency, site and duration are effective and safe for eczema; adverse effects are associated with inappropriate strength/site/duration. The reassurance is correctly conditioned on correct use, addressing common steroid-phobia without dismissing risk.
limitations: Safety is conditional on correct use, which the copy states.
reviewer_notes: Balanced. Reassurance is qualified. Acceptable.

page_title: Eczema, Psoriasis and Chronic Skin Conditions: Getting a GP Plan
claim_text: Can psoriasis affect more than skin? Yes. It can be associated with joint inflammation and other health risks ... your GP may also ask about joint pain, nails and cardiovascular risk.

supporting_source.org: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
supporting_source.title: Cardiovascular Risk in Patients With Psoriasis: JACC Review

evidence_summary: Psoriasis is associated with psoriatic arthritis (joint inflammation) and with increased cardiovascular risk driven by chronic inflammation and shared risk factors. The 'can be associated with' phrasing is exactly the correct (association, not causation) framing.
limitations: Absolute CV risk elevation is greatest in severe disease; the article does not quantify, which is appropriate for general information.
reviewer_notes: Uses 'associated with' correctly. Model wording. No change.

page_title: Eczema, Psoriasis and Chronic Skin Conditions: Getting a GP Plan
claim_text: Seek prompt care for rapidly spreading redness, fever, severe pain, swelling around the eyes, widespread blistering, a rash with purple spots that do not fade when pressed, or a child who is very unwell.
evidence_summary: A non-blanching purpuric rash (does not fade when pressed) plus fever is the classic meningococcal red flag; rapidly spreading redness, periorbital swelling and widespread blistering are correct urgent skin-infection/severe-reaction signs. All red flags are clinically correct and consistent with Australian guidance.
limitations: None material; list is a safe subset of red flags.
reviewer_notes: HIGH-risk clinical content verified correct. No change.

page_title: Eczema, Psoriasis and Chronic Skin Conditions: Getting a GP Plan
claim_text: Skin barrier: The outer protective layer of skin, often impaired in eczema. Is eczema always caused by allergy? No. Allergy can contribute for some people, but skin barrier, irritation, infection, climate and genetics also matter.
evidence_summary: Skin-barrier dysfunction is central to atopic eczema, and eczema is multifactorial (barrier, genetics, irritants, infection, environment) rather than purely allergic. Accurate.
limitations: None material.
reviewer_notes: Correctly corrects the common 'eczema = allergy' misconception.

page_title: Family GP Care in Maroubra: Why Continuity Matters
claim_text: A regular family GP can help join these pieces together ... Continuity ... means there is a trusted place to return to ... For adults, it helps with screening, mental health, lifestyle change and long-term risk reduction.

primary_source.org: British Journal of General Practice (Pereira Gray et al.)
primary_source.title: Primary medical care continuity and patient mortality: a systematic review

evidence_summary: Systematic-review evidence (Pereira Gray 2018/2020) links higher continuity of care with better outcomes and lower all-cause mortality across multiple countries, and RACGP endorses continuity. IMPORTANTLY, this article does NOT make the contested strong claim ('continuity reduces mortality'); it stays with proportionate benefits (joined-up care, screening, risk reduction). This is the safe position.
limitations: The mortality evidence is observational (cohort/cross-sectional), so causation is not proven - which is why the article's avoidance of a mortality claim is appropriate. Do NOT add a 'reduces mortality' claim to this copy.
reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM cleared: copy does not overstate. If future edits add 'continuity reduces mortality', downgrade to 'is associated with lower mortality in observational studies' and cite Pereira Gray.

page_title: Family GP Care in Maroubra: Why Continuity Matters
claim_text: Why does continuity help with children? Children change quickly. Seeing patterns over time can help identify growth, development, behaviour, allergy, eczema, asthma or family stress issues earlier.
evidence_summary: Longitudinal observation of a child's development and health patterns is a recognised benefit of continuity in general practice. 'Can help identify ... earlier' is proportionate.
limitations: General benefit statement, not a quantified outcome claim.
reviewer_notes: Acceptable.

page_title: GP, Urgent Care or 000? How to Decide in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs
claim_text: Call 000 immediately for chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, severe allergic reactions, stroke symptoms, collapse, severe bleeding, major trauma, drowning, poisoning, severe burns, prolonged seizures, a suicidal crisis with immediate danger, or any situation where life may be at immediate risk without emergency intervention.
evidence_summary: Each listed situation (chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, anaphylaxis, stroke, collapse/loss of consciousness, severe bleeding, major trauma, drowning, poisoning, severe burns, prolonged seizure, suicidal crisis with immediate danger) matches Healthdirect/Triple Zero guidance for calling an ambulance. Clinically correct and appropriately worded with 'immediately'.
limitations: The triplezero.gov.au link now issues a 301 redirect to https://infrastructure.gov.au/triple-zero (still resolves) - see GEN-13 for the link-maintenance flag.
reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM cleared: 000 advice is clinically correct. No wording change.

page_title: GP, Urgent Care or 000? How to Decide in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs
claim_text: Further reading link: [Triple Zero Australia](https://www.triplezero.gov.au/)
recommended_wording: Keep link text; the URL https://www.triplezero.gov.au/ now 301-redirects to https://infrastructure.gov.au/triple-zero - consider updating the href to the destination so it does not rely on the redirect.
evidence_summary: The linked URL resolves but only via a 301 permanent redirect. Content is authoritative and correct; this is a link-hygiene item, not a content error.
limitations: Redirect currently functions; no user impact today.
reviewer_notes: Minor maintenance: point href at the current canonical URL to be safe.

page_title: GP, Urgent Care or 000? How to Decide in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs
claim_text: 000: Australia's emergency number for ambulance, police or fire. ... If your condition deteriorates while waiting, do not drive yourself; contact emergency services instead.
evidence_summary: 000 is correctly described as the Australian emergency number for ambulance, police and fire. 'Do not drive yourself, call emergency services' is standard, correct safety advice for a deteriorating patient (e.g. suspected cardiac/stroke).
limitations: None material.
reviewer_notes: Accurate and safe.

page_title: How to Choose a GP in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs
claim_text: Do not wait for a routine GP appointment for chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, severe bleeding, sudden weakness on one side of the body, collapse, severe allergic reaction, serious injury or any life-threatening concern. Call 000.
evidence_summary: 'Sudden weakness on one side of the body' is a correct stroke red flag (F.A.S.T.); the remaining items match ambulance-call guidance. Clinically correct.
limitations: None material.
reviewer_notes: HIGH-risk content verified. No change.

page_title: How to Choose a GP in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs
claim_text: Dr Amanda Henderson is a local GP at GP Maroubra who provides caring, family-focused general practice close to home. ... What makes a good GP for a family? Look for someone who listens carefully, explains clearly, keeps good follow-up systems ...

primary_source.title: Advertising a regulated health service - guidelines

evidence_summary: Self-description uses non-comparative, verifiable language ('caring, family-focused general practice'). There is NO 'best GP', superiority, or comparative claim, and no patient testimonials, so it does not trigger the main AHPRA s.133 advertising prohibitions. Qualities are framed as general 'what to look for' advice, not exclusive claims.
limitations: AHPRA compliance is a regulatory matter, not a clinical evidence question; no legal conclusion is offered here.
reviewer_notes: Regulatory scan: no superiority/testimonial red flags found on this page. 'Caring/family-focused' is acceptable descriptive language.

page_title: How to Choose a GP in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs
claim_text: It is much easier to get good care when you have a regular doctor or practice that knows your background. Continuity matters for pregnancy planning, children's health, mental health, chronic conditions, contraception, preventive screening ...

supporting_source.org: British Journal of General Practice (Pereira Gray et al.)
supporting_source.title: Primary medical care continuity and patient mortality: a systematic review

evidence_summary: Continuity of care is associated with better preventive care uptake, chronic disease management and patient outcomes. 'Easier to get good care' is a proportionate, non-absolute benefit statement.
limitations: Observational evidence base (see GEN-10 limitations).
reviewer_notes: Acceptable; no mortality overstatement.

page_title: Lifestyle Medicine: Weight, Sleep, Alcohol, Smoking and Wellbeing
claim_text: Sleep apnoea: Interrupted breathing during sleep, often linked with snoring, tiredness and cardiometabolic risk.

primary_source.title: Caffeine, Food, Alcohol, Smoking and Sleep / OSA resources

evidence_summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea involves interrupted breathing during sleep, is associated with snoring and daytime tiredness, and untreated OSA is linked to cardiovascular/cardiometabolic risk. 'Often linked with' is correctly associational.
limitations: None material; definition is accurate.
reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM cleared. Uses 'linked with', not 'causes'. Acceptable.

page_title: Lifestyle Medicine: Weight, Sleep, Alcohol, Smoking and Wellbeing
claim_text: Can alcohol affect sleep even if it helps me fall asleep? Yes. Alcohol can fragment sleep and worsen snoring, reflux, mood and blood pressure.

primary_source.title: Caffeine, Food, Alcohol, Smoking and Sleep

supporting_source.title: Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol

evidence_summary: Sleep Health Foundation states alcohol may help falling asleep but disrupts sleep architecture causing fragmented sleep, and even modest amounts increase snoring and OSA frequency/intensity; alcohol also worsens reflux, mood and blood pressure. Fully supported.
limitations: Effect size varies with dose and individual; article gives no numeric guideline (so no NHMRC-number discrepancy risk).
reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM cleared. Accurate. Note: page does not quote specific NHMRC standard-drink limits, so no guideline-figure exposure.

page_title: Lifestyle Medicine: Weight, Sleep, Alcohol, Smoking and Wellbeing
claim_text: Sleep is poor and affecting mood, energy or concentration. ... [reasons to book]
evidence_summary: Poor sleep is bidirectionally associated with mood, energy and concentration, and can increase the risk of mood disorders (Sleep Health Foundation). Framed as a reason to seek help rather than a causal claim; proportionate.
limitations: Relationship is bidirectional; article does not overclaim direction.
reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM (sleep->mood) cleared. Acceptable.

page_title: Lifestyle Medicine: Weight, Sleep, Alcohol, Smoking and Wellbeing
claim_text: You want to reduce heart, diabetes, liver, cancer or mental health risk. ... Is weight always just about calories? No. Sleep, hormones, medications, mental health, pain, environment, genetics and life stress can all affect weight.

primary_source.title: Healthy living / reducing heart disease risk

supporting_source.title: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice (Red Book) - lifestyle risk factors

evidence_summary: Modifiable lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol, diet, activity, weight) are established contributors to cardiovascular, diabetes, liver, several cancer and mental-health risks, and weight regulation is genuinely multifactorial. Framed as patient goals ('you want to reduce ... risk') using 'reduce risk' rather than 'prevent'. Proportionate.
limitations: 'Reduce risk' is directional; no quantified risk reduction is claimed, which is appropriate.
reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM cleared. Uses 'reduce risk' correctly; multifactorial weight framing reduces stigma and is accurate.

page_title: Lifestyle Medicine: Weight, Sleep, Alcohol, Smoking and Wellbeing
claim_text: Can a GP prescribe medication for quitting smoking? Often yes ... Behavioural support and follow-up increase the chance of success.

primary_source.title: Supporting smoking cessation: A guide for health professionals

supporting_source.title: Combined pharmacotherapy and behavioural interventions for smoking cessation

evidence_summary: Combining pharmacotherapy with behavioural support and follow-up increases smoking-cessation success versus minimal support (RACGP; Cochrane). 'Increase the chance of success' is accurate and proportionate.
limitations: Suitability of pharmacotherapy is individual, which the copy states ('depending on your history and suitability').
reviewer_notes: Acceptable.

page_title: Lifestyle Medicine: Weight, Sleep, Alcohol, Smoking and Wellbeing
claim_text: Seek urgent help if you have chest pain, severe breathlessness, sudden weakness, suicidal thoughts, severe withdrawal symptoms, seizures, confusion, or if substance use is creating immediate safety risks.
evidence_summary: Severe alcohol withdrawal (seizures, confusion/delirium) is a medical emergency; chest pain, severe breathlessness, sudden weakness and suicidal thoughts are correct urgent red flags. Clinically correct.
limitations: None material.
reviewer_notes: HIGH-risk content verified. No change.

page_title: Men's Health Checks in the Eastern Suburbs: What to Ask Your GP
claim_text: Prostate screening is individual and should include a discussion of benefits, limitations and possible harms rather than a one-size-fits-all test. ... Should I have a prostate test? That decision should be individual. A GP can explain PSA testing, limitations and when further assessment is needed.

primary_source.title: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice (Red Book) - prostate cancer / PSA

supporting_source.title: Shared decision making in prostate cancer screening

evidence_summary: The RACGP position is that PSA testing is not recommended as routine population screening of asymptomatic men; where a man requests it, the GP should support an informed, shared decision covering benefits, limitations and harms (overdiagnosis/overtreatment). The article's framing - individual, shared decision, harms included, 'not one-size-fits-all' - is exactly the current mainstream Australian position and does NOT promote routine screening.
limitations: Guidance is contested internationally; some bodies differ. Australian position (RACGP; also RACGP/PSA testing pathway with Cancer Council Australia) is well represented here.
reviewer_notes: CONTESTED WATCH ITEM cleared: balanced, benefit/harm framing present, no overstatement of screening benefit. Model example of safe wording. No change.

page_title: Men's Health Checks in the Eastern Suburbs: What to Ask Your GP
claim_text: Bowel screening: Testing for hidden blood in stool for eligible people without symptoms. ... bowel cancer screening [as part of a men's health check].

primary_source.org: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
primary_source.title: National Bowel Cancer Screening Program

evidence_summary: The NBCSP uses an immunochemical faecal occult blood test (iFOBT) to detect hidden blood in stool in eligible people WITHOUT symptoms (currently ages 45-74, free every 2 years). The definition is accurate; the article wisely does not quote an age that could go stale.
limitations: Eligibility age changed to 45 from July 2024; article avoids stating an age so remains correct.
reviewer_notes: Accurate. Optional enhancement: could note the program is for ages 45-74, but current wording is safe.

page_title: Men's Health Checks in the Eastern Suburbs: What to Ask Your GP
claim_text: Cardiovascular risk: The chance of heart attack or stroke based on factors such as age, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking and diabetes.

primary_source.org: Australian Government / Australian Chronic Disease Prevention Alliance
primary_source.title: Australian CVD risk assessment guideline (cvdcheck.org.au)

evidence_summary: Australian CVD risk assessment estimates the probability of a heart attack or stroke from age, sex, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking status and diabetes. Definition is accurate.
limitations: Full risk calculators include additional variables; article gives a fair lay summary.
reviewer_notes: Accurate.

page_title: Men's Health Checks in the Eastern Suburbs: What to Ask Your GP
claim_text: Book promptly for blood in urine, black stools, unexplained weight loss, testicular lump, severe depression or suicidal thoughts. [and Call 000 for chest pain, severe shortness of breath, stroke-like symptoms, collapse or severe injury]
category: red flag / when to seek help

primary_source.title: Symptoms and when to seek help (blood in urine, testicular lump, weight loss)

evidence_summary: Blood in urine (haematuria), black/tarry stools (melaena), unexplained weight loss, and testicular lump are correct 'see a doctor promptly' warning symptoms; the 000 list (chest pain, severe breathlessness, stroke-like symptoms, collapse, severe injury) is clinically correct. Appropriately separates 'book promptly' from 'call 000'.
limitations: None material.
reviewer_notes: HIGH-risk content verified. Correctly triaged. No change.

page_title: Preventive Health Checks for Busy Adults
claim_text: Screening: Testing offered to people without symptoms when evidence supports benefit. ... Not every test is useful for every person; unnecessary testing can create confusion as well as reassurance.

primary_source.title: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice (Red Book)

evidence_summary: The RACGP Red Book frames screening as appropriate only where evidence supports net benefit, and explicitly warns against low-value/unnecessary testing (false positives, overdiagnosis). The article's definition and its acknowledgement of harms of over-testing align precisely with this evidence-based framing.
limitations: None material.
reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM (screening benefit) cleared: benefit AND harms both acknowledged. Exemplary framing.

page_title: Preventive Health Checks for Busy Adults
claim_text: Are full body scans useful for prevention? Usually not as a routine screening tool. A GP can explain which evidence-based checks are more useful for your risk.

primary_source.title: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice (Red Book)

evidence_summary: Routine whole-body scanning of asymptomatic people is not recommended (risk of false positives, incidentalomas, radiation, overdiagnosis) and is discouraged by RACGP and Choosing Wisely Australia. The article's 'usually not as a routine screening tool' is accurate.
limitations: None material.
reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM cleared. Correctly discourages low-value screening. No change.

page_title: Preventive Health Checks for Busy Adults
claim_text: The best preventive care is personalised. ... A GP can tailor screening to age, sex, family history, symptoms, culture, lifestyle, medical history and patient preference. Preventive care may include ... bowel screening, breast screening, cervical screening, vaccines ...

primary_source.title: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice (Red Book)

evidence_summary: Red Book preventive activities are explicitly individualised by age, sex, risk and preference; national programs exist for bowel, breast (BreastScreen) and cervical screening. Content accurate. 'Best preventive care is personalised' is a principle statement, not a comparative service claim, so no AHPRA superiority issue.
limitations: Referenced BreastScreen and National Cervical Screening Program links on the page are official health.gov.au program pages (stable).
reviewer_notes: Accurate and evidence-aligned.

page_title: Preventive Health Checks for Busy Adults
claim_text: Call 000 for chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, stroke symptoms, collapse, severe bleeding or life-threatening concerns. Book promptly for unexplained weight loss, blood in stool, breast lumps, persistent pain or severe mood symptoms.
category: emergency red flag / when to seek help
evidence_summary: 000 list is clinically correct; 'book promptly' symptoms (unexplained weight loss, blood in stool, breast lump, persistent pain, severe mood symptoms) are appropriate non-emergency warning signs. Correct triage separation.
limitations: None material.
reviewer_notes: HIGH-risk content verified. No change.

page_title: Travel Medicine and Vaccines: What to Discuss Before You Go
claim_text: How early should I book travel medicine advice? Ideally 6 to 8 weeks before travel, but later advice is still better than none. ... Some vaccines need more than one dose or time to work, so book early where possible.

primary_source.title: Getting vaccinated / before you go: health

evidence_summary: Standard travel-health guidance recommends a pre-travel consultation about 6-8 weeks before departure because some vaccines require multiple doses/time to reach full protection; last-minute advice still has value. The 6-8 week figure and multi-dose caveat are accurate.
limitations: Timing is a general recommendation; some itineraries need earlier planning.
reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM cleared. Specific timeframe verified. Acceptable.

page_title: Travel Medicine and Vaccines: What to Discuss Before You Go
claim_text: Malaria prophylaxis: Medicine used to reduce malaria risk when travelling to certain areas. ... They may discuss ... malaria prevention, mosquito avoidance, travellers' diarrhoea ...
evidence_summary: Antimalarial chemoprophylaxis reduces (does not eliminate) malaria risk in endemic areas and is combined with mosquito-bite avoidance. 'Reduce malaria risk' is correctly non-absolute (prophylaxis is not 100% protective).
limitations: Choice of agent depends on destination resistance patterns; correctly deferred to the GP.
reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM cleared. 'Reduce risk' framing is accurate.

page_title: Travel Medicine and Vaccines: What to Discuss Before You Go
claim_text: Seek urgent medical care during or after travel for fever after visiting a malaria area, severe dehydration, bloody diarrhoea, confusion, severe headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, animal bites, significant injuries or symptoms after possible rabies exposure.

primary_source.title: Avoiding infectious disease while travelling (malaria fever advice)

evidence_summary: Fever during or after travel to a malaria-endemic area is a medical emergency requiring urgent assessment (malaria can be rapidly fatal and can present weeks-months later); potential rabies exposure requires urgent post-exposure care as rabies is almost universally fatal once symptomatic. All listed travel red flags are clinically correct.
limitations: None material; list is a safe, correct subset.
reviewer_notes: HIGH-risk travel content verified. No change.

page_title: Travel Medicine and Vaccines: What to Discuss Before You Go
claim_text: Check Smartraveller for current destination advice as well as seeing a GP. [links: Smartraveller, Australian Immunisation Handbook, healthdirect]
evidence_summary: Smartraveller (smartraveller.gov.au), the Australian Immunisation Handbook and healthdirect are correct, authoritative Australian sources; all three referenced URLs resolve. Signposting to Smartraveller for current destination advice is appropriate.
limitations: Body text spells the service 'Smartraveller' (correct); ensure consistency across the site.
reviewer_notes: Correct sources. Minor copy note: keep 'Smartraveller' spelling consistent (one word, two 'l's).

page_title: Acne Treatment for Teens and Adults: When to See a GP
claim_text: Seek urgent care for severe allergic reactions or symptoms such as lip or tongue swelling, breathing difficulty or collapse.

supporting_source.org: ASCIA (Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy)
supporting_source.title: Anaphylaxis signs (swelling of tongue/throat, difficulty breathing)

evidence_summary: Lip/tongue swelling, breathing difficulty and collapse are correct anaphylaxis red flags requiring emergency care. Clinically accurate.
limitations: None material.
reviewer_notes: HIGH-risk content verified. No change.

page_title: Family GP Care in Maroubra: Why Continuity Matters
claim_text: Dr Amanda Henderson is a GP consulting at GP Maroubra ... she provides family-focused general practice care across pregnancy and pre-pregnancy health, shared antenatal care, women's health, contraception, paediatrics, lifestyle medicine, travel medicine, men's health and preventive care. [repeated on all 9 pages]

primary_source.title: Advertising a regulated health service - guidelines

evidence_summary: This standardised block appears on all nine pages and describes the range of general-practice services offered. It contains no comparative/superiority claims ('best', 'leading', 'expert'), no guarantees of outcome, and no patient testimonials, so it does not raise the main AHPRA advertising prohibitions. The male-health/men's-health scope offered by a female GP is unremarkable in general practice.
limitations: This is a regulatory/factual-accuracy observation, not a legal conclusion. Practice should ensure the listed services are actually provided/available (factual-accuracy requirement).
reviewer_notes: Cross-cutting regulatory scan across all 9 assigned pages: NO 'best GP'/superiority language, NO testimonials, NO unqualified prevention/cure claims found. Confirm all listed services are genuinely offered to satisfy the 'not false or misleading' standard.
